A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, Machine Unlearning Fails to Remove Data Poisoning Attacks. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original unlearning experiments on CIFAR-10 and IMDb, plus logistic and synthetic linear regression experiments investigating unlearning failure.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds membership-inference comparisons, SSD evaluations, dimensionality sensitivity, targeted-attack reliability results, and runtime measurements.

M1.justification: Gaussian poison generation and the averaged Gaussian Unlearning Score remain unchanged. However, the proposed membership decision changes from |I_z| > tau in v1 Section 4.3 and Appendix A.1.4 to I_z > tau in v2 Section 4.3 and Appendix B.1, a limited procedural revision.

E1.justification: Both versions use CIFAR-10 image classification, IMDb sentiment analysis, and the same regression settings. The IMDb attack renamed 'backdoor' in v2 was already evaluated in v1. Resolution and target-sampling experiments remain within existing coverage; the new tabular-compatibility claim does not establish an additional evaluated dataset.

E2.justification: v2 adds SSD to the CIFAR-10 Gaussian and targeted comparisons, SCRUB to the targeted CIFAR-10 comparison, and NGD to the indiscriminate-results table. It also directly evaluates the loss-threshold MIA attributed to Shokri et al. against Gaussian auditing in Figures 2 and 10, substantially expanding comparison methods.

E3.justification: The principal training and unlearning budgets remain unchanged. Additional protocols include varying image dimensions from 26x26x3 to 32x32x3 while unlearning 1,000 points, sweeping SSD's selection parameter, and testing 100 randomly selected targets. The reported Gaussian membership threshold also changes; these revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of Gaussian auditing's dependence on input dimensionality (Figure 8), SSD hyperparameter sensitivity (Figure 9), and targeted poisoning's reliability across selected targets (Appendix E.2). Figures 2 and 10 additionally examine failures of standard MIA evaluation. The original compute-budget, forget-set-size, and model-shift analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The eight vision runs, five language runs, and usual ±1 standard deviation reporting remain unchanged. However, the stated null distribution of the averaged Gaussian score changes from N(0,1/P) in v1 Algorithm 4, line 24, to N(0,1) in v2 Algorithm 2, line 24, changing its reported statistical calibration without changing the averaging.

E6.justification: v2 adds MIA comparisons, SSD outcomes, dimensionality trends, runtime results, and a reported 71.2% targeted-attack failure rate in Appendix E.2. NGD's targeted CIFAR-10 poison success changes from 66.67% in v1 Figure 3a to approximately 33% in v2 Figure 4a. Gaussian TPR bars also change alongside the revised decision rule. Shared indiscriminate-table entries and earlier forget-set ablations remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix B.3 extends v1's illustrative Gaussian-score calculation with a normal approximation and Neyman-Pearson power derivation. Figure 7 corrects the displayed TPR expression by adding the missing '1 minus'. The averaged-score null variance also changes, and the new edge-case derivation uses a normalization inconsistent with the retained score definition. These are bounded mathematical revisions.

C1.justification: The central claim that existing approximate unlearning methods fail to reliably remove poisoning remains. v2's introduction expands the evaluated-method count from seven to eight, explicitly claims compatibility with tabular data, and promotes the already-present failure hypotheses into the contribution list. The abstract and conclusion retain substantially the same claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of why forget-set performance is an unreliable evaluation criterion, why higher input dimensionality may improve Gaussian auditing, and why targeted poisoning can be too brittle for evaluation. Appendix D.2.8 interprets SSD's disagreement with earlier studies through attack differences, while Appendix C expands applicability and access-requirement claims. The original model-shift hypotheses remain.

D1.justification: v2 announces access to Gaussian-poisoning code through OpenUnlearn, identifies the authors' implementation used for SSD, documents its parameters, and adds approximate runtimes in Table 5. Most existing optimizer settings, learning rates, poisoning instructions, and training budgets are retained. The linked code's availability was not externally verified.

R1.justification: Section 2 shifts emphasis from direct versus indirect influence toward detection power and evaluation cost. Appendix A substantially expands comparisons with verification and graph-unlearning work, including Wu et al. (2023), and elaborates the already-cited Marchant and Sommer work. SSD discussion adds positioning against Foster and Schoepf et al.; duplicate or publication-updated references are not counted as new works.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites Section 3 around evaluation preliminaries, condenses the algorithm descriptions, introduces a dedicated standard-MIA results subsection, and relocates substantial related-work and implementation material. The appendices are reorganized into separate related-work, Gaussian-analysis, methodological-comparison, implementation, experimental, and failure-analysis sections.

P2.justification: The main dual-axis plots are redesigned into separate accuracy and unlearning-efficacy panels. v2 adds comparison and sensitivity figures, expands the knowledge-requirements table, and adds methodological and runtime tables. The original cosine-similarity figure moves to Appendix F as Figure 14, while retained ablation plots are consolidated within the new conference layout.

improvement.justification: The direct MIA comparisons, SSD sensitivity analysis, additional diagnostics, and code disclosure strengthen empirical support and reproducibility. However, v2 does not reconcile its new signed Gaussian threshold with the negatively shifted scores retained in Figure 6, and Algorithm 2 changes the averaged score's null variance from 1/P to 1 without rescaling. These inconsistencies affect the central audit, leaving the net quality change uncertain.
